items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: I did one on “Stella By Starlight” that featured Charlie Mariano on alto sax

ctx.x: Are there a couple of Kenton arrangements that you feel stand out as your most successful?

I did one on “Stella By Starlight” that featured Charlie Mariano on alto sax, and that came off very well, and I also did around the same time, this was 1955, I did one on “Stompin’ at the Savoy,” which has kind of stood up. We still play it with my band now. So I think those two stand out to me.

I have a couple of things that I wanted to play for you. Actually I think it’s a bit early for that, because I wanted to ask about the first time — you had quite a list of singers here that you arranged for also. And when was your first experience doing a chart for a singer?

items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I asked Charlie about this idea of writing a longer piece for the quintet, and he was all for it.

ctx.x: Okay. If it‟s not something that‟s currently on your mind, then I‟ll start with a couple of things that I felt that should be included in the chronology, and that is the composition Quartet, for Shelly Manne‟s quintet, written in 1956, or at least recorded in 1956. This is quite an adventurous piece. It‟s written in four movements. Maybe you could talk about the inspiration and the writing of that particular work.

I wanted to bring to a small jazz band the idea of a longer work, and utilizing the concept of form, which isn‟t really a big consideration with most small jazz groups. Charlie Mariano, who is one of my all-time favorite alto players, was in the band at that time. I had been in Shelly‟s group earlier, the end of 1955, or actually when he formed it in ‟55. I had left, because I had writing to do, and I didn‟t feel that I could give it all the concentration that it needed, because I knew that he wanted to have a…

Okay. I wanted to look at – the personnel in the band other than Charlie Mariano: Stu Williamson, playing trumpet and trombone – valve trombone, that is. He‟s not a name that we consider a household name. Maybe you could talk a little bit about Stu, because he appears on a lot of sessions and seemed to be working pretty regularly.
